title: Why You Should Stand In One Place While Giving Directions iving-directions/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the conventional wisdom that teachers should move around the room to keep students engaged, arguing instead that standing still while giving directions produces better attention and comprehension. He explains that a consistent physical location becomes associated with listening, that movement itself is a distracting stimulus, and that stillness lets a teacher accurately gauge whether the message is landing. He distinguishes this from lesson delivery, where movement and passion are appropriate, reserving stillness specifically for routines, directions, and daily announcements. The piece frames the change as small but immediately noticeable in how well students track and understand what's said.
points: Giving directions from the same consistent spot builds an association that primes students to listen and apply what follows.
Movement and extraneous arm gestures compete with a teacher's voice as sources of distraction during directions.
Standing still lets a teacher read attentiveness in real time and confirm the message is actually landing.
Stillness during directions should be paired with active eyes and facial expressions to stay connected to all students at once.
Movement is appropriate during passionate lesson delivery, but not during routines, directions, or daily announcements.
quotes: Conventional wisdom says that you move around the room to keep your students engaged and involved.
But the surprising truth is that your students will become more attentive if you stand still and in one place while giving directions.
When you give directions from the same place, day after day, your students will associate that place with listening, understanding, and applying what you tell them.
Any movement or stimulation outside of your calm, clear voice is a distraction.

Whenever you have directions to give or information to share, if you stay rooted to the most visible and accessible place in your classroom, your students will listen, pay attention, and understand what you say better and more accurately than when you move.
